- After World War I, levain was abandoned entirely in favor of yeast and the invention of the baguette a few years later, yet the basic method of “building” a piece of dough set aside from the last batch with two or three additions of flour and water remained unchanged in Southwest France in the 1920s and persisted in some areas of France for much longer. [painaulevai3WY, page ?]  

- Lesaffre updated levain cultures to be more acidic to comply with new French legislation; many loaves were forgettable, and pain au levain must be well made; Parmentier’s message was “take care of the levain!”. [painaulevai3, page ?]  

- Hubert Chiron noted that levain varies from baker to baker; the acidity level must remain reasonable; darker flours and levain work marvelously; Pain Virgule cooperative (formed 1992) delivers loaves from organic stone‑ground flour. [painaulevain9WY, page ?]  

- Extreme acidity and lightness result from very warm dough temperatures and prolonged fermentation; a culture over 100 years old can produce a pain au levain that tastes like the usual one; Parmentier’s 1778 book contains many partial understandings; salt slows fermentation; an ailing levain cannot be revived by wine or vinegar. [painaulevain11, page ?]
